title: Lutetium-177 oxodotreotide (Lutathera / PRRT)
context_label: Progressive, unresectable or metastatic, well-differentiated G1/G2 somatostatin-receptor-positive gastroenteropancreatic NET under NCCP 00642a.
purpose: PRRT carries radiation to somatostatin receptors on NET cells to help control disease that cannot be removed or has spread. A specialist NET and nuclear-medicine team checks receptor imaging, organ function and your priorities before recommending it.
schedule_summary: Four administrations are planned, usually eight weeks apart. Lutathera is infused over about 30–40 minutes, with a four-hour kidney-protective amino-acid infusion and anti-sickness treatment. The visit is much longer than the Lutathera infusion; an overnight stay may be needed.
scope_note: This guide covers the Irish NCCP G1/G2 SSTR-positive GEP-NET regimen. A receptor scan, specialist eligibility review and individual radiation-safety plan are required.
schedule_label: Four planned administrations, usually every eight weeks
indication_text: NCCP 00642a: progressive unresectable or metastatic well-differentiated G1/G2 SSTR-positive GEP-NET. Specialist selection is required.
phases_note: Four administrations are intended, not guaranteed. Blood results, recovery, specialist review and the service plan determine whether and when each can be given.
timeline_note: The 56-day view shows a usual interval, not a guarantee of the next administration. The radiation band shows a possible period only; each restriction has its own written end date from the service. Symptoms and abnormal tests can persist after any band ends.
safety_note: Follow your oncology unit’s emergency instructions. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice; do not wait for the next appointment. Call emergency services for collapse, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain or uncontrolled bleeding.
teachback: Can you explain the four planned visits, your blood-test timetable, the separate SSA injection plan, radiation precautions and who to call for sudden hormone symptoms?
consent_support: Discuss the exact SSTR-positive NET indication, benefit and uncertainty, alternatives, kidney and marrow injury including delayed MDS/leukaemia, hormone crisis, tumour lysis, fertility/pregnancy, radiation precautions and the monitoring and SSA plan.
urgent_extra: Seek urgent help for sudden severe flushing with faintness, severe diarrhoea, wheeze or breathing trouble, especially in the first 48 hours; follow the hormone-crisis plan. Fever, bleeding, much less urine, persistent severe abdominal pain, muscle weakness or confusion needs prompt advice. Tell emergency staff when you received PRRT; radiation precautions must not delay urgent care.

agents.name: Lutetium-177 oxodotreotide
agents.mechanism: Carries radiation to somatostatin receptor targets
agents.explanation: Lutathera joins a receptor-binding molecule to the radioactive element lutetium-177. After infusion, it attaches to somatostatin receptors on suitable NET cells and delivers radiation nearby. The receptor scan helps select patients. Kidneys and blood-forming marrow can also receive radiation, which is why kidney protection and long-term blood monitoring matter.
agents.watch: Keep all between-treatment and after-treatment blood tests; use your personalised radiation-safety and hormone-symptom plans.
risks: Nausea, vomiting, appetite loss and fatigue
Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Hormone crisis and tumour lysis syndrome
Delayed marrow disorders including MDS and acute leukaemia
Fertility effects, pregnancy harm and radiation exposure to others

agents.name: Lysine / arginine amino acids
agents.explanation: The amino-acid infusion reduces the amount of radioactive medicine retained in the kidneys. It is an essential part of kidney protection. It can cause nausea and affect potassium or fluid balance, so anti-sickness treatment, blood tests and observation are needed.
agents.watch: Tell staff promptly about nausea, palpitations, weakness, breathlessness or swelling during infusion.

passport_visit_note: Record administrations T1–T4, blood tests, scan appointments, SSA timing and exact radiation-precaution end dates. A stamp records an administration; it does not approve the next one.
anatomy: Tiredness may last beyond the treatment day. Severe weakness, confusion, seizure or collapse needs urgent assessment.
Nausea and vomiting can occur, especially around treatment. Tell staff early and follow the anti-sickness and fluid plan.
Potassium or fluid changes can affect the heart. Report palpitations, new swelling or breathlessness promptly; severe symptoms are an emergency.
Counts may fall during or after the course. Report fever, bruising or bleeding. Rare late marrow disorders require ongoing follow-up.
Liver tests are monitored before, between and after treatments. Report yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or persistent severe abdominal pain.
Amino acids reduce kidney exposure but do not remove risk. Keep renal blood tests and report much less urine or dehydration.
Abdominal pain, diarrhoea or sudden hormone release can occur. Severe flushing, faintness, diarrhoea or wheeze needs urgent advice.
Discuss fertility before treatment. Avoid pregnancy using the written contraception plan; follow individual radiation precautions for close contacts.
anatomy_note: Selected regimen-specific effects anchored to the full-body illustration. Blood, hormone and skin effects can involve more than one area. This is not a prediction or a complete side-effect list.
administration_text: The standard NCCP activity is 7.4 GBq by intravenous infusion, usually every eight weeks for four administrations; the specialist may alter, delay or stop treatment. Lutathera runs over approximately 30–40 minutes. A lysine/arginine amino-acid infusion starts 30 minutes beforehand and continues for four hours. An anti-sickness medicine is given at least 30 minutes before the amino acids.

phases.label: Four planned PRRT administrations
phases.detail: Usually eight weeks between administrations, with blood tests every two weeks and a PRRT clinic review. The service confirms each date and any delay.

timeline.label: PRRT and protective infusions
timeline.text: Anti-sickness treatment, amino acids and Lutathera; admission / overnight plan confirmed.

timeline.label: Personal radiation-safety plan
timeline.text: Restriction periods differ by activity and contact; follow your written end dates, not the band alone.

timeline.label: Fortnightly blood tests and PRRT review
timeline.text: Blood count, kidneys and liver; dates are booked individually.

timeline.label: Assessment for next administration
timeline.text: Usually eight weeks later; proceed only after specialist approval.

day_groups.title: Treatment and early observation
day_groups.body: Plan a long hospital visit; the first treatment generally involves an overnight stay. Staff give anti-sickness medicine and kidney-protective amino acids. Hormone reactions are especially important in the first 48 hours.
day_groups.action: Before discharge, obtain written emergency contacts, SSA timing and radiation precautions.

day_groups.title: Recovery and individual precautions
day_groups.body: Energy, appetite and bowel symptoms may change. Radiation precautions may last two to three weeks for some activities or contacts; exact restrictions come from the medical physicist.
day_groups.action: Attend blood tests every two weeks. Call for fever, bleeding, reduced urine, severe pain or sudden hormone symptoms.

day_groups.title: Tests and next-treatment decision
day_groups.body: Continue fortnightly bloods and attend the PRRT review. A post-infusion scan checks radiation distribution; response scans follow a separate specialist plan.
day_groups.action: The team confirms whether and when the next administration is suitable. Do not treat an eight-week date as automatic clearance.

support.title: Kidney protection
support.text: A lysine/arginine infusion is required for kidney protection and begins before Lutathera. Follow the service’s fluid and toileting advice. Tell staff about heart or kidney problems; do not use a generic fluid target.

support.title: Nausea prevention
support.text: PRRT has moderate emetogenic potential. A 5-HT3 anti-sickness medicine is given at least 30 minutes before the amino-acid infusion, with additional treatment if needed. Tell staff promptly if nausea starts.

support.title: Somatostatin analogue coordination
support.text: Long-acting SSA injections can interfere with receptor targeting. NCCP uses a 30-day interval before PRRT and short-acting injections are withheld for 24 hours. The referring NET consultant decides your exact stop and restart plan, balancing hormone control. Never stop injections on your own.

support.title: Radiation safety and practical planning
support.text: The medical physicist gives individual written and verbal advice. Contact with young children or pregnant people may need restriction for up to three weeks, and close-contact work may require up to two weeks away. Arrange transport, sleeping, toileting, laundry and caring responsibilities before admission.

monitoring_schedule.title: PRRT tests before, between and after four intended administrations

rows.label: Blood count / kidneys / liver
cells: Baseline tests
Once 2–4 weeks beforehand AND shortly before infusion
Every 2 weeks
Every 4 weeks for at least 3 months, then every 3 months for the following year
Additional tests or longer follow-up if abnormal

rows.label: Potassium / renal clearance
cells: Assess renal function and electrolyte risks
Potassium before amino acids; renal function and suitability reviewed
Renal checks during therapy; earlier assessment if ill
Renal monitoring for at least the first year
Fluid and electrolyte plan individualised

rows.label: Heart / pregnancy / hormones
cells: ECHO or MUGA; pregnancy testing where applicable; hormone plan
Review symptoms and any pregnancy possibility; SSA plan confirmed
Report hormone symptoms, especially during first 48 hours
Follow hormone symptoms and contraception plan
Additional heart tests if clinically indicated

rows.label: Imaging / clinic
cells: SSTR-positive disease and baseline assessment
Specialist clearance for each treatment
PRRT clinic review; special scan(s) after each infusion for radiation assessment
Response and follow-up imaging as agreed
No universal mandatory tumour-marker or response PET interval

cells: Discuss household, travel, work and care needs
Receive written instructions for this administration
Observe each restriction until its own end date
Keep discharge information and tell other treating teams
Medical physicist confirms personal restrictions

monitoring_schedule.note: This is the NCCP blood-test sequence with EMA potassium safety and the Irish PRRT service pathway. The post-infusion radiation-assessment scan is different from a response scan. The service confirms bookings, exact dates and any additional follow-up.

monitoring_summary: Baseline blood count, kidneys/liver, ECHO/MUGA and pregnancy assessment where applicable. Counts/kidneys/liver once 2–4 weeks before and shortly before each infusion, every two weeks between, then every four weeks for at least three months after the final dose and every three months for the following year. Potassium is checked before amino acids. Renal monitoring continues at least through the first year. Post-infusion radiation scans and response scans have separate purposes.

chronology_notes.title: Four administrations, not four consecutive days
chronology_notes.text: The intended administrations are usually eight weeks apart. Record each actual date and any change; delays do not authorise a catch-up treatment.

chronology_notes.title: Two kinds of scan
chronology_notes.text: The Irish service describes special scans after each infusion to measure radiation delivered to organs. CT/MRI or other scans to assess tumour response follow the specialist plan.

chronology_notes.title: Follow-up extends beyond the fourth treatment
chronology_notes.text: Blood counts, kidneys and liver require continued checks. Kidney injury and rare marrow disorders may appear later, so retain the follow-up schedule and report new symptoms.

chronology_notes.title: Radiation safety has individual end dates
chronology_notes.text: A contact restriction, work restriction and sleeping arrangement may finish on different dates. The wallet or calendar is a reminder; your written radiation-safety instructions control the details.

sections.title: Before admission
sections.text: Confirm SSTR imaging, appointments, recent bloods, hormone medicines and pregnancy precautions. Tell the team about kidney/heart problems, incontinence, a catheter, childcare or close contact with pregnant people; these may change the practical plan.

sections.title: Treatment day
sections.text: The standard NCCP activity is 7.4 GBq by intravenous infusion, usually every eight weeks for four administrations; the specialist may alter, delay or stop treatment. Lutathera runs over approximately 30–40 minutes. A lysine/arginine amino-acid infusion starts 30 minutes beforehand and continues for four hours. An anti-sickness medicine is given at least 30 minutes before the amino acids. The first visit generally includes an overnight stay; later treatments may be day case or overnight. The service confirms your plan.

sections.title: SSA injections: stop and restart
sections.text: The NET and nuclear-medicine teams must coordinate the injection plan. Do not translate “about four weeks” into your own date: NCCP specifies 30 days for long-acting SSA and 24 hours for short-acting SSA before PRRT. Restart timing follows the written service plan; it can differ with day-case arrangements.

sections.title: At home after treatment
sections.text: Follow individual instructions on distance and time with other people, sleeping arrangements, toilets, body fluids, laundry, work and transport. Restrictions may extend to three weeks for some contacts. Contact the medical physicist before discharge if you cannot follow the plan at home.

sections.title: Travel and other healthcare
sections.text: Carry the discharge letter and treatment card, including the date and type of radioactive treatment. Ask about travel and radiation detectors. Tell any healthcare staff you have had PRRT; urgent care must never be delayed because of radiation precautions.

sections.title: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility
sections.text: Lutathera can harm an unborn child and may affect fertility. Discuss fertility preservation before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for seven months after the last dose for patients who could become pregnant; men with partners who could become pregnant need contraception during treatment and for four months afterwards. Breastfeeding must stop before treatment; follow specialist advice.

sections.title: If a visit is delayed
sections.text: The team decides whether a delayed administration remains suitable and whether activity must change. Do not assume a treatment can automatically proceed at the maximum interval. Continue the blood-test and symptom plan.

sections.title: Contacts and paperwork
sections.text: Write the actual NET, PRRT nursing and radiation-protection contacts on the paper plan. Example numbers are not clinical contact lines. Keep the written precautions and urgent hormone-symptom instructions with the discharge letter.

sections.title: The Irish service’s scan appointments
sections.text: The detailed Irish leaflet describes three radiation-assessment scans on separate days in the first week after the first infusion, starting the next day, and one scan after later infusions. It also describes CT or MRI between the second and third infusions and after the course. These are service arrangements to confirm on your appointment sheet, not a universal timetable for every NET.

sections.title: Extra blood tests after the course
sections.text: NCCP specifies four-weekly blood tests for at least three months, then three-monthly for the following year. The Irish service leaflet also describes fortnightly tests for eight weeks immediately after the final infusion. Your written discharge plan may therefore require more frequent early tests; follow that plan and ask the service to resolve any mismatch.

sections.title: Paper radiation instructions for home
sections.text: Before discharge, obtain a paper copy with the exact end date for each restriction. The Irish leaflet includes daily bathing, careful handwashing, sitting to pass urine and separate washing of body-fluid-soiled laundry in the first week. Ask for specific handling instructions for pads, incontinence or a catheter. Sleeping, travel, work and contact limits differ: examples include separate beds from a partner for 14 days and sleeping apart from pregnant people or children for three weeks. Your medical physicist’s personal instructions take precedence.

sections.title: Carry the official radiation card too
sections.text: The medical physicist supplies a radiation-treatment card to carry for the time stated. The SACTCheck wallet card is an additional treatment record and does not replace that official card, the discharge letter or the radiation-safety plan.

evidence.title: What NETTER-1 did and did not show
evidence.intro: The trial studied progressive SSTR-positive midgut NET after octreotide treatment.
evidence.population: Adults with advanced well-differentiated SSTR-positive midgut NET progressing on long-acting octreotide.
evidence.interpretation: Lutetium-177 DOTATATE with standard-dose octreotide improved time before progression compared with high-dose octreotide.
limitations: The final overall-survival comparison was not statistically significant. The findings do not promise a survival gain for an individual.

NETTER-1 was a midgut study. Its results must not be presented as identical evidence for every pancreatic, other GI or grade 3 NET. The current Irish eligibility and specialist decision determine this regimen’s use.

chapters.title: Your PRRT course
chapters.intro: Receptor-directed radiation with specialist safety checks.

chapters.title: Blood tests, scans and follow-up
chapters.intro: Tests continue between treatments and after the course.

items.title: The full safety-test sequence
items.text: Baseline blood count, kidneys/liver, ECHO/MUGA and pregnancy assessment where applicable. Counts/kidneys/liver once 2–4 weeks before and shortly before each infusion, every two weeks between, then every four weeks for at least three months after the final dose and every three months for the following year. items.title: What may change treatment
items.text: The specialist may postpone, reduce or stop treatment for low counts, kidney/liver abnormalities, other toxicity or disease change. A four-stamp record shows intended administrations; it cannot confirm medical suitability.

items.title: Post-treatment scans
items.text: The Irish service describes special scans after each infusion to measure radiation delivered to organs. CT/MRI or other scans to assess tumour response follow the specialist plan.

items.title: Delayed effects
items.text: Kidney injury and rare bone-marrow disorders, including myelodysplastic syndrome or acute leukaemia, can occur later. Persistent tiredness, infections, bruising or bleeding needs review even after the treatment course.

chapters.title: Urgent symptoms, hormone safety and precautions

items.title: When to seek help
items.text: Seek urgent help for sudden severe flushing with faintness, severe diarrhoea, wheeze or breathing trouble, especially in the first 48 hours; follow the hormone-crisis plan. Fever, bleeding, much less urine, persistent severe abdominal pain, muscle weakness or confusion needs prompt advice. Tell emergency staff when you received PRRT; radiation precautions must not delay urgent care.

items.title: Hormone crisis
items.text: PRRT can trigger a sudden hormone release. The Irish leaflet highlights the first 48 hours as the main early-risk period. Staff monitor you and may give extra medicines or extend the stay. You need clear instructions for symptoms after discharge; a history of hormone symptoms affects planning.

items.title: Tumour breakdown and fluid changes
items.text: Rapid tumour breakdown can disturb blood chemistry. New muscle cramps, weakness, confusion, palpitations, reduced urine or breathlessness needs prompt assessment. Staff also monitor potassium and fluid balance around the amino-acid infusion.

items.title: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility
items.text: Lutathera can harm an unborn child and may affect fertility. Discuss fertility preservation before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for seven months after the last dose for patients who could become pregnant; men with partners who could become pregnant need contraception during treatment and for four months afterwards. chapters.title: Understanding your particular NET
chapters.intro: Several different features help the team choose treatment.

items.title: Where it started and where it is now
items.text: A neuroendocrine tumour (NET) starts in cells that receive signals and can release hormones. The original organ is the primary site. A pancreatic NET is different from the more common pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Stage describes how far the cancer has spread; the stage system depends on its original site. A tumour in the liver may be a NET that spread there from elsewhere.

items.title: Differentiation, grade and Ki-67
items.text: Differentiation describes how the cells look under the microscope. Grade describes their growth activity. Ki-67 is a laboratory measure of the proportion of tumour cells showing a marker of cell growth and helps assess grade in relevant NETs. It is not the percentage of your body affected and is not a survival percentage. Ask for the exact pathology wording, grade and Ki-67 result, including the sample date.

items.title: Grade is different from stage
items.text: A low-grade NET can have spread, and a high-grade tumour is not automatically stage 4. Well-differentiated grade 3 NET and poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma are different diagnoses with different treatment choices. These medicine guides must not be applied to another diagnosis simply because its name contains neuroendocrine.

items.title: Functioning and nonfunctioning
items.text: A functioning NET causes a hormone-related syndrome. A nonfunctioning NET does not cause a recognisable excess-hormone syndrome, but it can still grow or cause symptoms by its size or location. Ask which description applies to you. A positive somatostatin receptor scan does not by itself mean the tumour is functioning.

items.title: Your diagnosis record
items.text: Keep the primary site, differentiation, grade, Ki-67 if reported, stage or sites of spread, hormone syndrome and receptor-scan result together in your passport. Ask the team to explain changes rather than trying to interpret one result in isolation.

chapters.title: Making sense of tests and results
chapters.intro: Safety tests, tumour tests and hormone tests answer different questions.

items.title: Blood tests for treatment safety
items.text: Blood counts measure infection-fighting cells, oxygen-carrying cells and platelets. Kidney and liver tests help the team assess how your body can handle treatment. The schedule for your medicine is shown separately. Attend these checks even when you feel well; a scan does not replace them.

items.title: CT, MRI and receptor imaging
items.text: CT and MRI help show tumour size and where it is. A somatostatin receptor (SSTR) scan looks for receptor targets that certain treatments can attach to. An FDG-PET scan answers a different question about tumour activity and may be useful in selected cases. You will not necessarily need every scan. The specialist decides which test can change your care.

items.title: Hormones and tumour markers are individual
items.text: The team may measure selected blood or urine markers when they answer a question about your NET or symptoms. These can include serotonin-related testing such as 5-HIAA for selected patients, or specific pancreatic hormones. Chromogranin A is not a universal test before every treatment. A changing marker alone does not prove cancer growth. Record why each test is being done, how to prepare and who will explain it.

items.title: Preparing for a test
items.text: Ask whether you need fasting, a timed urine collection, dietary preparation or a medicine review. Follow the laboratory’s instructions for your particular test. Do not stop an acid-suppressing medicine, diabetes medicine or hormone-control treatment yourself. Tell the team about kidney problems, allergies and all medicines before a scan or blood test.

items.title: Heart and inherited-risk checks
items.text: A heart ultrasound may be needed for particular treatment risks or to assess heart-valve problems associated with a hormone syndrome. It is not required on the same timetable for every NET. Depending on the diagnosis, age and family history, the team may offer genetic counselling; some NETs occur with inherited conditions such as MEN1. A tumour gene test and an inherited-risk test are not interchangeable.

items.title: Who does what, and when?
items.text: Use the passport to write each test, its purpose, planned date, booking service, result-review contact and next step. Your consultant sets response-scan and marker intervals. The postoperative schedules in general guides are not automatically the right schedule while you are taking these medicines.

chapters.title: Hormone symptoms and day-to-day changes
chapters.intro: A new symptom may come from the NET, treatment or another illness.

items.title: Build a picture of what is normal for you
items.text: Record your usual bowel pattern, flushing, pain, appetite, weight and energy before starting. Note what changes, how long it lasts, what you were taking and how it affects daily life. This helps the team distinguish a hormone problem from treatment toxicity without assuming that every symptom is cancer progression.

items.title: Hormone-related symptoms
items.text: Depending on the tumour, excess hormones may cause flushing, frequent watery stools, wheezing, acid-related pain or blood-sugar disturbances. An insulin-producing tumour can cause low blood sugar. Not every NET causes these problems. Ask which symptoms matter for your diagnosis and whether you need a separate rescue plan.

items.title: Hormone treatment is a separate part of the plan
items.text: Somatostatin analogue injections and other symptom treatments may continue alongside anticancer treatment when prescribed. They may have their own appointment dates. Never stop them simply because tablets are paused. PRRT requires a carefully coordinated interruption and restart plan, which the nuclear-medicine service must supply.

items.title: When a change is urgent
items.text: Follow your oncology emergency plan for sudden or severe symptoms. Collapse, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion or uncontrolled bleeding needs emergency assessment. Severe diarrhoea, persistent vomiting, dehydration, fever or sudden illness needs urgent oncology advice. Do not wait for a scan, an online answer or the next clinic visit.

items.title: Procedures and hormone syndromes
items.text: Tell the surgical, dental, anaesthetic or imaging team if you have a hormone-producing NET or a previous hormone crisis. Ask your specialist whether special preparation is needed. Carry your current medicines and emergency plan; the wallet card supports this information but does not replace specialist instructions.

chapters.title: Your overall plan and choices
chapters.intro: Your priorities belong in the treatment plan.

items.title: What are we trying to achieve?
items.text: Ask whether the main aim is to slow growth, reduce tumour size, relieve hormone symptoms, make another treatment possible or protect day-to-day quality of life. The aim and likely benefit depend on your particular NET and previous treatment. A stable scan may represent useful control even without tumour shrinkage.

items.title: How treatments fit together
items.text: Some people need surgery, hormone-control treatment, tablets, chemotherapy, PRRT, liver-directed treatment or external radiotherapy at different points. These are not all automatically part of your regimen. Ask the multidisciplinary team to draw your own sequence and name the clinician coordinating it.

items.title: Choosing between options
items.text: Ask why this option suits your tumour site, grade, growth rate, symptoms, receptor status and other health conditions. Discuss alternatives, the option of observation when appropriate, supportive care, and any suitable clinical trial. A treatment listed in a US guide is not a guarantee of availability or funding in Ireland.

items.title: Evidence is about groups
items.text: A trial can measure time before cancer worsens, tumour shrinkage or survival. These are different outcomes. A group result does not predict your own response or lifespan. Ask how closely the study patients match your diagnosis and what benefit would make the treatment worthwhile to you.

items.title: Review points and shared decisions
items.text: Agree when you will review symptoms, tests and scans, and what would lead to continuing, delaying, changing or stopping treatment. Discuss work, caring duties, travel and the effects you most want to avoid. You can revisit your choices as your situation changes.

chapters.title: Eating, energy, practical help and support
chapters.intro: Supportive care can be used alongside treatment from the start.

items.title: Food, weight and digestion
items.text: Tell the team about weight loss, poor appetite, early fullness, persistent diarrhoea or greasy stools. Ask for a dietitian familiar with NETs and your surgery or medicines. Different causes need different support; do not assume every bowel symptom needs the same diet or medicine. Ask whether digestive-enzyme assessment or replacement is relevant to you.

items.title: Fluids and safe activity
items.text: Follow your individual fluid advice, especially with diarrhoea, kidney disease or heart problems. Balance manageable activity with rest. Tell the team if fatigue, dizziness, pain or breathlessness limits usual tasks; these symptoms can have treatable causes.

items.title: Emotions, relationships and quality of life
items.text: Living with repeated tests and treatment can affect sleep, mood, relationships and confidence. Ask about psychological support, sexual health, fertility advice, symptom-control services and support for carers. Supportive or palliative care aims to improve comfort and daily life and can accompany active anticancer treatment.

items.title: Practical help
items.text: Ask your nurse or social worker about transport, work, finances, home support, caring responsibilities and local NET support organisations. A general resource list may include services in other countries; your team can identify options available to you.

items.title: A record that works without a phone
items.text: Keep the printed schedule, medicine list, tests, contact numbers and written emergency instructions together. The full handbook contains the information in sequence for offline reading. The QR code is an optional route to more information; it is not needed to call for help or follow your paper plan.

items.title: Questions to take to the next visit
items.text: What is my exact diagnosis and grade? What is treatment trying to achieve? Which tests are mandatory for this medicine, and which depend on my NET? Who reviews results? What symptoms mean call now? What support would help me live as well as possible?

questions.q: Does my receptor scan and exact NET diagnosis meet this PRRT indication?
questions.a: The specialist team must confirm progressive, well-differentiated G1/G2 SSTR-positive GEP-NET and assess other eligibility factors. A receptor scan alone does not establish that treatment is suitable.

questions.q: Will the first or later visits require overnight admission?
questions.a: The Irish leaflet describes an overnight stay for the first treatment; later treatments may be day case or overnight. Confirm the actual admission and discharge plan with the PRRT service.

questions.q: Who provides the written stop/restart dates for my SSA injections?
questions.a: The referring NET consultant and nuclear-medicine team coordinate the injection plan. Get exact written dates; do not stop or restart an SSA on your own.

questions.q: When are my fortnightly and post-course blood tests?
questions.a: NCCP specifies two-weekly bloods between administrations and continued tests after the course. The Irish service may arrange additional early post-course checks. Ask for one reconciled written schedule and result-review contact.

questions.q: Which household, work and travel precautions apply, and on what dates do they end?
questions.a: The medical physicist gives individual restrictions, which can extend to three weeks for some contacts. Obtain each end date and discuss transport, sleeping, childcare and work before admission.

questions.q: What symptoms suggest a hormone crisis, and who do I call after discharge?
questions.a: Sudden severe flushing, faintness, diarrhoea, wheeze or breathing trouble can require urgent assessment, particularly in the first 48 hours. Follow the service’s written emergency plan and do not delay urgent care because of radiation precautions.

questions.q: What fertility, contraception and long-term follow-up plan do I need?
questions.a: Discuss fertility before starting. Current EMA/HSE information requires contraception during treatment and for seven months afterwards for patients who could become pregnant, and four months for men with partners who could become pregnant. Blood and organ-function follow-up continues after the fourth administration.

patient_summary.purpose: Specialist receptor-targeted radiation for selected advanced NETs.
patient_summary.schedule: Four planned administrations, usually 8 weeks apart; each needs specialist clearance.

phases.title: Treatment day
phases.text: Anti-sickness medicine, 4-hour kidney-protective amino acids and a 30–40-minute PRRT infusion. Overnight stay may be needed.

monitoring.when: Counts, kidneys/liver; ECHO/MUGA; pregnancy assessment where applicable.
Counts, kidneys/liver 2–4 weeks before AND shortly before; potassium before amino acids.
Counts, kidneys/liver every 2 weeks. Special scans after each infusion.
Every 4 weeks for ≥3 months, then every 3 months for the following year; service may arrange earlier extra tests.

cycle_expectations: Follow the written SSA injection and radiation-safety plans; some contact restrictions last up to 3 weeks.
Urgent help for severe flushing, faintness, wheeze or diarrhoea, especially first 48 hours; report fever, bleeding or reduced urine.
preparation: Arrange home/work precautions and actual emergency contacts before admission. Scans for tumour response follow your specialist plan.
patient_summary.card_schedule: Four planned administrations, usually 8 weeks apart. Keep blood tests and written radiation precautions.
patient_summary.card_record_note: T1–T4 record actual administrations. A stamp does not approve the next treatment. Keep each radiation restriction’s end date. Carry the official radiation card too.
patient_summary.card_alert: Carry your official radiation card too. Tell staff your last PRRT date; do not delay urgent care.

treatment_scope_notice: Specialist G1/G2 SSTR-positive GEP-NET PRRT. Use the service’s written appointment, SSA, radiation-safety and emergency instructions.
